newsitem.title: FRANCE: French paedophilia probe going overboard - minister.
newsitem.headline: French paedophilia probe going overboard - minister.

text.p: French Justice Minister Elisabeth Guigou suggested on Monday that police and media had gone overboard in a mass crackdown on paedophilia which has prompted the suicide of four suspects.
Paedophilia is "abominable...and the pursuit of suspects must be carried out without delay and without hesitation," she told Europe 1 radio.
"Yet I wonder whether we need these spectacular arrests and all this media attention."
A total of 323 people have been placed under investigation and 24 remanded in custody in a nationwide operation involving 2,500 police. Those rounded up have included teachers and clergymen.

The highly publicised raids initially targeted some 800 individuals whose names were found on a computerised mailing list of a firm based in the central city of Macon which sold pornographic video cassettes involving under-age boys.
The suicides have triggered an emotional debate over police tactics and the meaning of justice.
The Paris-based League of Human Rights accused investigators of unnecessarily humiliating suspects.
But Macon prosecutor Jean-Louis Coste said human rights activists should be most concerned about children who suffered abuse.
"They are the ones who need attention first," Coste told RTL radio.
In a statement entitled "a prosecutor scorning principles", the League hit back.
"The fight against acts of paedophilia...does not mean exposing dozens of people to public condemnation, to the point of provoking four suicides," it said.

One of the suspects told France Inter radio he had appeared on the mailing list after contacting the firm to buy films that were legally available, unaware that it also sold illicit pornographic material.

A lawyer for the family of one of the four people who committed suicide has said he will file a lawsuit to find out how the suspect's name leaked to the media. The body of Gilbert Pic, who threw himself into the Garonne river on Saturday from a bridge in the southwestern city of Bordeaux, was found on Monday.
"When magistrates use the press to puff themselves up, I think it neither honours justice nor the press," lawyer Benoit Ducos-Ader said on Sunday.

Henri Leclerc, a lawyer who is president of the League of Human Rights, said the paedophilia probe had become "a witch hunt...based on passion rather than reason". He pleaded for "justice rather than a lynching".

Leclerc told the daily Liberation that some suspects were totally innocent. "They were detained in the round-up, they were later released, but they are done for," he said. "Their image has been destroyed for ever."
